title: Orbits in the Schwarzschild geometry
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Extends the Schwarzschild motion analysis from radial plunges to orbits with angular momentum: proves motion stays in a plane, dresses the radial equation as a Newtonian-looking effective potential with one extra -M L^2/r^3 term, reads off circular, scattering, capture and precessing orbits (including the 6M innermost stable orbit and the L/M = 4 capture threshold), shows Kepler's third law survives in coordinate time, derives the orbit equation dr/dphi, perturbs it about a Newtonian ellipse to get a perihelion advance of 6 pi M/r0 per orbit, and applies it to Mercury's 43 arcsecond per century anomaly.
role_in_book: Third of the Part IV chapters on the Schwarzschild exterior. Chapter 20 built Newtonian orbits (effective potential, u = 1/r, eccentricity), Chapter 21 produced the Schwarzschild metric, and Chapter 22 supplied the conserved quantities E-tilde and L-tilde, the effective-potential form of the radial equation, and the L = 0 radial plunge. This chapter switches angular momentum on and delivers the first classical solar-system test of the theory, perihelion precession. It sets up Chapter 24, which repeats the effective-potential method for photons (light bending, photon sphere, the unstable circular orbit flagged here), and Chapter 25 on black holes, where the capture orbits found here no longer end on a stellar surface. The exercises also seed the idea, returned to repeatedly in the book, that the rubber-sheet picture misses the time part of curvature.

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild line element in Schwarzschild coordinates, geometric units G = c = 1
Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass E-tilde and L-tilde from the time and phi symmetries of the metric
Effective potential form of the Schwarzschild radial equation and the radial plunge with L = 0
Newtonian effective potential, turning points, circular orbits, the u = 1/r substitution and the conic solution u = u0(1 + epsilon cos theta)
Four-velocity normalization u.u = -1 for massive particles and proper time as the geodesic parameter
Geodesic equations obtained by varying the line element (Euler-Lagrange route)
Raising and lowering indices with a diagonal metric and its inverse
Kepler's laws and the Newtonian Kepler problem
Binomial expansion to first order and simple harmonic oscillator solutions
Stability of equilibria from maxima and minima of a potential
Astronomical scales: solar mass, Mercury's orbit radius and period, arcseconds
Embedding diagrams for curved 2D surfaces (needed for Exercise 23.5)

learning_objectives: Reader can show from the theta geodesic equation that an orbit starting with theta = pi/2 and zero polar velocity stays in the equatorial plane, and link this to angular momentum conservation.
Reader can write the Schwarzschild radial equation as effective energy (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 = (dr/dtau)^2/2 + V_eff and identify which term in V_eff has no Newtonian counterpart.
Reader can locate the extrema r_+ (stable, outer) and r_- (unstable, inner) of V_eff and explain how their existence depends only on L-tilde/M.
Reader can explain why stable circular orbits require L-tilde/M >= sqrt(12) and do not exist inside r = 6M.
Reader can show that at L-tilde/M = 4 the potential peak sits at r = 4M with V_eff = 0, and use this to sort incoming unbound particles into scattered and captured.
Reader can classify orbits (circular, bound precessing, scattering, capture/spiral-in) by drawing an energy line across a sketch of V_eff.
Reader can combine the circular-orbit conditions to obtain L-tilde^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M), E-tilde^2 and L-tilde/E-tilde, and deduce that (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^3 exactly as in Kepler's third law.
Reader can derive the orbit equation dr/dphi from u.u = -1 and the two conserved quantities without solving the full geodesic equations.
Reader can rewrite the orbit equation in u = M/r as a Newtonian equation plus relativistic correction terms and justify keeping only the leading one.
Reader can obtain the perihelion advance delta phi = 6 pi M/r0 per orbit by rescaling the angle so the perturbed equation becomes a harmonic oscillator.
Reader can restore G and c and estimate Mercury's relativistic perihelion shift (about 41-43 arcseconds per century) and place it in the budget of the total observed precession.

Reader can explain that the precession comes partly from spatial curvature (about one third) and mostly from the g_tt part of the metric (about two thirds), and why this undercuts the rubber-sheet picture.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, Newtonian-parallel chapter. Every relativistic formula is deliberately written to look like its Chapter 20 counterpart so that the learner only has to track the differences: one extra attractive r^-3 term in the effective potential, and extra correction terms in the u-equation for the orbit. Orbit types are taught graphically with side-by-side panels pairing a potential curve plus energy line with the resulting trajectory. Formal Example boxes carry the algebra (plane confinement, circular-orbit relations, the massaged orbit equation, the Mercury numbers). The perihelion result is obtained by an order-of-magnitude argument that discards the smaller correction and then a variable rescaling that turns precession into a mismatch between the radial period and 2 pi. The physical interpretation (space curvature versus time curvature) is only sketched in the text and farmed out to two guided exercises, one using Flamm's paraboloid and a cone-wedge picture, the other a toy metric with only g_tt modified.
narrative_arc: Motivation: Newtonian ellipses were a triumph, but GR's first success was improving on them; relax the L-tilde = 0 restriction of Chapter 22 to allow angular motion.
Simplify: prove from the theta equation that orbits can be taken in the equatorial plane without loss of generality (Example 23.1).
Model: reuse the effective-energy form of the radial equation and the Schwarzschild V_eff; point to the -M L^2/r^3 term as the single new ingredient.
Analyse the potential: find the two extrema r_+ and r_- from V_eff' = 0 and show everything depends on L-tilde/M (Fig. 23.1).
Classify motion graphically: circular, scattered and captured trajectories paired with their energy lines (Example 23.2, Fig. 23.2); contrast with the Newtonian infinite centrifugal wall.
Read off thresholds: L-tilde/M = sqrt(12) gives an inflection and the smallest stable circular orbit at 6M; L-tilde/M = 4 puts the peak at V_eff = 0 so marginally unbound particles cannot bounce.
Circular orbits quantitatively: derive L-tilde^2/r^2, E-tilde^2 and L-tilde/E-tilde (Example 23.3), then show Kepler's third law holds unchanged in coordinate time.
Formalism for general orbits: from u.u = -1 and the conserved quantities get dr/dtau, then divide by dphi/dtau to get the orbit equation dr/dphi (23.15), with the Newtonian version in a margin note.
Check against Newton: in u = M/r, massage the orbit equation into Newtonian form plus two correction terms and compare their sizes (Example 23.5).
Solve: keep the leading correction, rescale the angle, and read off that one radial period takes more than 2 pi of azimuth, giving delta phi/2 pi = 3M/r0 (Fig. 23.4).
Application: restore constants for Mercury, compare with the 43 arcsecond anomaly and the full 575 arcsecond budget; history of failed Newtonian fixes and Einstein's reaction (Example 23.6).

Interpretation: precession arises partly from spatial curvature shortening the orbit and mainly from curvature in the time part, so it is a spacetime effect; exercises quantify the one-third/two-thirds split.
signature_moves: Newtonian mirror: equations are arranged so that each relativistic formula sits beside its Newtonian analogue (margin notes 2 and 8), and the learner hunts for the extra terms.
Paired visual panels: every orbit type is shown as a V_eff curve with a horizontal energy line on the left and the corresponding orbit shape on the right.
Threshold numbers read directly off one dimensionless ratio L-tilde/M (sqrt(12) and 4), rather than a zoo of cases.
Avoids the second-order geodesic equations entirely: normalization of u plus two conserved quantities give dr/dtau and dphi/dtau, whose ratio is the orbit shape.
Order-counting in powers of u0 and epsilon to justify discarding a correction term before solving.
Rescaled angle psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi, which turns the perturbed orbit into an exact oscillator and makes the precession a period mismatch.
Full observational bookkeeping for Mercury (total precession, planetary part, solar oblateness, residual) plus the human story of the anomaly.
Decomposes a relativistic effect into space-curvature and time-curvature parts using deliberately artificial metrics in the exercises, reinforcing the book's warning about rubber-sheet pictures.
Ends with a programming exercise that asks learners to integrate the orbit equation numerically, including handling the sign flip at turning points.

sections.title: Chapter opening: from plunges to orbits
sections.summary: Opens with an epigraph from Hobbes about a leap into the dark and recalls that Newtonian orbit theory was a crowning success, while one of GR's earliest wins was predicting orbits close to, but measurably different from, Kepler ellipses. Orbits are described as periodic geodesics. The chapter will reuse the Schwarzschild line element and the conserved quantities E-tilde and L-tilde from Chapter 22, dropping the earlier restriction to zero angular momentum, and will end with perihelion precession. A margin panel restates the line element and the definitions of E-tilde and L-tilde.
concepts: conserved angular momentum per unit mass
key_moves: Frame orbits as a special class of geodesics executing periodic motion
Announce the relaxation of L-tilde = 0 from the radial plunge
Recall the conserved quantities as the main tools

sections.title: Orbits for massive particles
sections.summary: Massive-particle orbits are timelike geodesics parametrized by proper time. Example 23.1 uses the theta geodesic equation to show that equatorial motion with no initial polar velocity stays equatorial, the relativistic version of planar Kepler motion. The radial equation is written in effective-energy form with E = (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2, and the Schwarzschild effective potential is quoted from Example 22.1: Newtonian gravity and centrifugal terms plus an extra attractive -M L^2/r^3 term that matters most for large M, large L and small r. Its extrema r_+ (a Newton-like minimum) and r_- (a maximum with no Newtonian analogue) follow from V_eff' = 0 and depend only on L-tilde/M (Fig. 23.1). Example 23.2 and Fig. 23.2 show a circular orbit at the minimum, an incoming particle bouncing off the peak, and a higher-energy particle clearing the peak and spiralling inward, which cannot happen in Newtonian gravity where the centrifugal wall is infinitely high. For L-tilde/M below sqrt(12) there is only an inflection and no stable orbit; for L-tilde/M = 4 the peak is at r = 4M with V_eff = 0, so particles arriving from infinity cannot be scattered unless L-tilde exceeds 4M.
concepts: relativistic r^-3 term in the effective potential
key_moves: Theta equation d/dtau(r^2 dtheta/dtau) = r^2 sin theta cos theta (dphi/dtau)^2 is solved by theta = pi/2 for all tau
Radial equation in Newtonian form: E = (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r)
Identify -M L^2/r^3 as the sole new term and when it is large
Solve V_eff'(r) = 0 as a quadratic to get r_+/- = (L^2/2M)[1 +/- (1 - 12M^2/L^2)^{1/2}]
Classify motion with an energy line: where E = V_eff the radial velocity vanishes but the particle still moves in phi
Contrast: Newtonian barrier deflects every particle with L != 0; Schwarzschild barrier has finite height so energetic particles are captured
Threshold cases L/M = sqrt(12) (inflection) and L/M = 4 (peak at 4M touches V_eff = 0)

sections.title: Stable circular orbits
sections.summary: Stable circular orbits sit at the potential minimum r_+, which exists only for L-tilde/M >= sqrt(12); at that limiting value r_+ = 6M, the smallest radius for a stable circular orbit. A margin note adds that the potential maximum is an unstable circular orbit, previewing the photon case in Chapter 24. Example 23.3 sets dr/dtau = 0 and E = V_eff to get E-tilde^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2), combines it with the extremum condition to find L-tilde^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M), E-tilde^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(r - 2M)/(r - 3M), and a formula for (L/E)^2. Dividing dphi/dtau by dt/dtau then gives dphi/dt in terms of L/E, and substituting yields (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^3, so Kepler's third law for circular orbits is unchanged when time is Schwarzschild coordinate time.
concepts: energy and angular momentum of circular Schwarzschild orbits
Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild spacetime
key_moves: Circular orbit = minimum of V_eff with E equal to V_eff(r_+)
Smallest stable radius 6M at L-tilde/M = sqrt(12)
Eliminate L between E = V_eff and V_eff' = 0 to get L^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M)
Compute E-tilde^2 and (L/E)^2 (printed 23.6 and 23.9 contain slips; see gaps)
Angular velocity as ratio dphi/dt = (dphi/dtau)/(dt/dtau) = (1/r^2)(1 - 2M/r)(L/E)
Result (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^3 identical to Newton-Kepler

sections.title: Precession of the perihelion
sections.summary: Introduces perihelion precession as one of the three classical solar-system tests (with light bending and gravitational redshift; Shapiro delay as a fourth). Example 23.4 and Fig. 23.3 show a bound particle oscillating between two turning points in V_eff while its near-elliptical orbit rotates, forming a rosette. The orbit equation is built without the full geodesic equations: u.u = -1 with the inverse metric and conserved quantities gives (dr/dtau)^2, eqn 23.14; dphi/dtau = L/r^2; their ratio gives dr/dphi, eqn 23.15, the master equation for Schwarzschild paths, printed beside the Newtonian version. Example 23.5 moves to u = M/r, rewrites the equation as the Newtonian circle-offset form ((u')^2 + (u - u0)^2 - epsilon^2 u0^2) plus two relativistic terms 6u0(u - u0)^2 and 2(u - u0)^3, identifies u0 with the circular-orbit radius of eqn 23.4, and argues the cubic term is smaller by a factor epsilon. Keeping the quadratic correction, the substitution psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi makes the radial motion periodic with period 2 pi in psi, so one radial cycle spans Delta phi = 2 pi (1 - 6M/r0)^{-1/2}, about 2 pi (1 + 3M/r0), i.e. delta phi = 6 pi M/r0 per orbit (Fig. 23.4). Example 23.6 restores G and c for Mercury: about 4.8 x 10^-7 rad per orbit, about 41 arcsec per century, versus a more careful GR value of 43.0 and an observed residual of 43.1 +/- 0.5 out of about 575 total, 532 from other planets and 0.03 from solar oblateness. The closing paragraph attributes precession partly to spatial curvature shortening the orbital path and mainly to curvature of the time part, a genuine spacetime effect; a margin note warns that rubber-sheet models show only the spatial half.
concepts: classical solar-system tests of general relativity
near-Newtonian expansion of the orbit equation
angle rescaling for the perturbed orbit
space and time contributions to perihelion precession
key_moves: Use u.u = -1 plus conserved E-tilde and L-tilde instead of the full geodesic equations
Lower/raise indices: g^{rr}(u_r)^2 = g_{rr}(u^r)^2 for a diagonal metric
Solve for (dr/dtau)^2 (23.13-23.14) and divide by dphi/dtau = L/r^2 to get dr/dphi (23.15)
Substitute u = M/r to get (du/dphi)^2 as a cubic in u (23.17)
Complete the square about u0 to expose Newtonian form plus corrections (23.18-23.21), matching 6u0 to eqn 23.4
Order counting: 6u0(u-u0)^2 ~ u0^3 epsilon^2 kept, 2(u-u0)^3 ~ u0^3 epsilon^3 dropped
Rescale psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi so the equation is an oscillator in psi with period 2 pi
Delta phi = 2 pi/(1 - 6M/r0)^{1/2} ~ 2 pi(1 + 3M/r0), so delta phi = 6 pi M/r0
Restore constants: delta phi = 6 pi G M_sun/(c^2 r0) for Mercury and convert to arcseconds per century
Physical reading: spatial curvature plus (dominant) temporal curvature

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The two-bullet summary stresses that orbits follow from E-tilde, L-tilde conservation and u^2 = -1, and that perihelion precession is a classical test passed with excellent agreement. Seven exercises follow: proper orbital period of a circular orbit two ways; a circular orbit in an exponentially expanding de Sitter-type metric; t versus tau for a particle held at fixed r; the acceleration of a prescribed circular world line and when it vanishes; isolating the spatial-curvature share of precession via Flamm's paraboloid and a cone-wedge argument (delta about 2 pi M/r); isolating the g_tt share with a flat-space, curved-time metric (two thirds of the total); and a numerical trajectory integrator for L-tilde/M = 4.3.
concepts: space and time contributions to perihelion precession
proper period of a circular orbit
numerical integration of the orbit equation
key_moves: Summary reduces the chapter to conserved quantities plus normalization
Exercises 23.5 and 23.6 split the precession into a one-third spatial and a two-thirds temporal share
Exercise 23.7 turns eqn 23.15 into a computational lab

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The unique static, spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations outside a mass M; in Schwarzschild coordinates and geometric units ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Not rederived; restated in a margin panel at the chapter start as the geometry in which all orbits here are computed. Its inverse components are listed in a margin note for the u.u = -1 calculation.

concepts.name: conserved energy per unit mass
concepts.definition: E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau, the constant of geodesic motion associated with time-translation symmetry of Schwarzschild spacetime; it equals the particle's energy per unit rest mass measured by a static observer at infinity, so E-tilde > 1 for particles that can reach infinity with nonzero speed.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 22 via the opening margin panel; used to set the energy line in effective-potential plots and to eliminate dt/dtau from the normalization condition.

concepts.name: conserved angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.definition: L-tilde = r^2 sin^2(theta) dphi/dtau, the constant of geodesic motion associated with rotational symmetry about the polar axis; in the equatorial plane L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dtau.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 22; the chapter's novelty is allowing L-tilde to be nonzero. Its ratio to M controls the whole shape of the effective potential.

concepts.name: four-velocity normalization
concepts.definition: For a massive particle parametrized by proper time, g_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu = -1; this first integral of the geodesic equation replaces the radial second-order geodesic equation when conserved quantities are available.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the first line of the orbit-equation derivation, written with the inverse metric and lowered components u_t = -E-tilde, u_phi = L-tilde, then solved for (u^r)^2.

concepts.name: plane confinement of Schwarzschild orbits
concepts.definition: A free particle in Schwarzschild spacetime moves in a plane through the centre; choosing coordinates so the initial position and velocity lie in theta = pi/2, the theta geodesic equation keeps theta = pi/2 for all proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Proved in Example 23.1 from the theta Euler-Lagrange equation: at theta = pi/2 the source term sin theta cos theta vanishes, so r^2 dtheta/dtau stays at its initial value zero. Linked to angular momentum conservation, as in the Newtonian case.

concepts.name: effective energy variable
concepts.definition: The combination (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2, chosen so that the exact Schwarzschild radial equation takes the Newtonian form of kinetic plus potential energy per unit mass; it is negative for bound motion and positive for particles that reach infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from Chapter 22 so that energy lines can be drawn on V_eff plots exactly as in Chapter 20; margin note 3 explains the sign for particles from infinity.
concepts.notes: It is not the kinetic plus potential energy of the particle; the Newtonian appearance is a bookkeeping device valid in proper time.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild effective potential
concepts.definition: The function V_eff(r) = -M/r + L^2/(2r^2) - M L^2/r^3 (per unit mass, geometric units) that governs radial motion in proper time for a massive particle with specific angular momentum L-tilde around a Schwarzschild mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from Example 22.1 and deliberately compared with the Newtonian effective potential energy in margin note 2; plotted for several L-tilde/M in Fig. 23.1 and used as the stage for all orbit classification.
prerequisites: conserved angular momentum per unit mass

concepts.name: relativistic r^-3 term in the effective potential
aliases: relativistic correction to the centrifugal barrier
concepts.definition: The extra attractive term -M L-tilde^2/r^3 in the Schwarzschild effective potential. It dominates the centrifugal term at small r, so the angular momentum barrier has finite height and eventually turns over, creating a maximum, an innermost stable orbit, capture orbits and precession.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out right after the potential is written as the source of everything new; the authors note it grows with M and L-tilde and at small r.
concepts.notes: In ordinary units the term is -GM L^2/(c^2 r^3); it is a correction of relative size roughly L^2/(c^2 r^2), i.e. (v/c)^2 for orbital speed.

concepts.name: extrema of the effective potential
concepts.definition: The radii where V_eff'(r) = 0: an outer minimum r_+ (stable circular orbit) and an inner maximum r_- (unstable circular orbit), given by r_+/- = (L^2/2M)[1 +/- (1 - 12M^2/L^2)^{1/2}]; they are real only if L-tilde/M >= sqrt(12) and merge at 6M when equality holds.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by setting the derivative of V_eff to zero, which gives a quadratic in r; the dependence on L-tilde/M alone is emphasized as the relativistic echo of the Newtonian case.
concepts.notes: The book calls these turning points of the potential; in orbit language 'turning points' normally means radii where the energy line meets V_eff.

concepts.name: stable circular orbit
aliases: circular orbit at the potential minimum
concepts.definition: An orbit of constant r at the minimum r_+ of V_eff with effective energy equal to V_eff(r_+) (negative, hence bound); small radial perturbations oscillate about it.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown first in Fig. 23.2(a) as a dot at the bottom of the potential well paired with a circle; quantified in Example 23.3.

concepts.name: innermost stable circular orbit
aliases: minimum radius for stable circular orbits
concepts.definition: In Schwarzschild spacetime no stable circular orbit exists inside r = 6M; at r = 6M the potential minimum and maximum merge into an inflection, which happens for L-tilde/M = sqrt(12).
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from eqn 23.4 and Fig. 23.1: for L-tilde/M below sqrt(12) = 3.464 there is only an inflection, not enough angular momentum to hold an orbit; the limiting minimum lies at 6M.
concepts.notes: The acronym ISCO is not used in the book. At 6M, E-tilde = sqrt(8/9), so a particle spiralling in through circular orbits radiates about 5.7 percent of its rest energy (our computation from eqn 23.8, not in the text).

concepts.name: unstable circular orbit
aliases: circular orbit at the potential maximum
concepts.definition: A circular orbit at the potential maximum r_-; any small perturbation sends the particle either inward to capture or outward, so it is dynamically unstable. For massive particles it lies between 3M and 6M.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in margin note 5 as the counterpart of the minimum, with a pointer to the photon analogue (the photon sphere) in Chapter 24.
concepts.notes: The 3M lower bound is our addition: from L^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M), circular orbits need r > 3M.

concepts.name: scattering orbit
concepts.definition: An unbound trajectory (effective energy > 0) whose energy line meets the inner potential barrier, so the particle comes in from infinity, reaches a minimum radius, and returns to infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 23.2(b) and Example 23.2: incoming particle hits the peak of V_eff and is sent back out; its orbit sketch loops around the centre.

concepts.name: capture orbit
concepts.definition: A trajectory whose effective energy exceeds the maximum of V_eff (or for which no maximum exists), so the radius decreases through the barrier and the particle spirals into the central object; absent in Newtonian gravity for any nonzero angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 23.2(c) and Example 23.2, contrasted explicitly with the Newtonian infinite centrifugal barrier at small r.
prerequisites: relativistic r^-3 term in the effective potential
concepts.notes: The book assumes a star is present to crash into; for a black hole the particle crosses r = 2M (Chapter 25).

concepts.name: critical angular momentum L = 4M
concepts.definition: For L-tilde = 4M the maximum of V_eff lies at r = 4M with height exactly zero, so particles arriving from infinity (effective energy > 0) cannot be turned back; only for L-tilde > 4M can some incoming particles be scattered.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked from eqn 23.4 in a short paragraph of §23.1 and backed by margin note 4 (such particles spiral in).
concepts.notes: The threshold is energy dependent: more energetic particles need larger L-tilde to be scattered. The circular orbit at 4M with E-tilde = 1 is the marginally bound orbit (term not used in the book).

concepts.name: energy and angular momentum of circular Schwarzschild orbits
concepts.definition: For a circular geodesic at radius r: L-tilde^2 = M r^2/(r - 3M), E-tilde^2 = (1 - 2M/r)^2 r/(r - 3M), and (L-tilde/E-tilde)^2 = M r (1 - 2M/r)^{-2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 23.3: impose dr/dtau = 0 and V_eff' = 0, eliminate between them.
prerequisites: conserved angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.notes: The printed eqn 23.9 has r_+^2 where r_+ is correct; see gaps.

concepts.name: Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild spacetime
concepts.definition: For circular geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime the angular velocity with respect to Schwarzschild coordinate time obeys (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^3, identical in form to the Newtonian result.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived straight after Example 23.3 by dividing dphi/dtau by dt/dtau and inserting L/E; the authors state the outcome matter-of-factly as identical to Kepler's own law and conclude relativity leaves the third law for circular orbits untouched.
prerequisites: energy and angular momentum of circular Schwarzschild orbits
concepts.notes: The simplicity depends on using coordinate time t (clock at infinity) and the areal radius r; proper period and proper circumference differ (Exercise 23.1).

concepts.name: bound precessing orbit
concepts.definition: A bound orbit with effective energy between the potential minimum and the smaller of zero and the maximum, oscillating between periapsis and apoapsis radii while the azimuth advances by more than 2 pi per radial cycle, so the near-ellipse rotates.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 23.4 and Fig. 23.3 (exaggerated precession) pair the two turning points on V_eff with the dotted boundary circles of a rosette.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild orbit equation
concepts.definition: The first-order equation for the spatial shape of an equatorial geodesic, dr/dphi = +/-(r^2/L){[-1 + E^2(1 - 2M/r)^{-1} - L^2/r^2](1 - 2M/r)}^{1/2}, obtained from normalization and the conserved quantities.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in §23.3 by solving u.u = -1 for (dr/dtau)^2 and dividing by dphi/dtau = L/r^2; printed beside its Newtonian counterpart (23.16) and used to draw Figs. 23.2-23.3.
prerequisites: conserved angular momentum per unit mass
concepts.notes: The sign must be switched at each turning point when integrating numerically (Exercise 23.7).

concepts.name: Binet substitution u = 1/r
concepts.definition: Replacing r by u = 1/r (or dimensionless u = M/r) turns orbit equations into polynomial equations in u, where Newtonian conic orbits become simple harmonic motion in phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 20 in margin note 8 and applied as u = M/r in Example 23.5; margin note 9 warns not to confuse it with the four-velocity u.

concepts.name: near-Newtonian expansion of the orbit equation
aliases: relativistic corrections to the Newtonian orbit equation
concepts.definition: Rewriting the relativistic (du/dphi)^2 equation around the circular-orbit value u0 as the Newtonian ellipse equation plus correction terms 6u0(u - u0)^2 and 2(u - u0)^3, then keeping only the dominant correction by comparing orders in u0 and eccentricity epsilon.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 23.5: expand, match coefficients to fix u0 (which reproduces eqn 23.4) and E0, introduce epsilon by analogy with the Newtonian definition, and estimate term sizes.
prerequisites: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem
concepts.notes: u0 is the relativistic circular-orbit value M/r_+, not the Newtonian GMm^2/L^2; epsilon plays the role of eccentricity only approximately.

concepts.name: angle rescaling for the perturbed orbit
concepts.definition: Absorbing the correction factor into a new angle psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi so that the linearized orbit equation becomes an exact oscillator with period 2 pi in psi; the physical azimuth per radial period is then 2 pi/(1 - 6u0)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Used immediately after Example 23.5 to solve eqn 23.22 and read off the precession.
prerequisites: near-Newtonian expansion of the orbit equation

concepts.name: perihelion precession
concepts.definition: The rotation of a bound orbit's closest-approach point in the orbital plane; for a Schwarzschild orbit the perihelion advances by delta phi = 6 pi M/r0 per orbit to first order in M/r0, where r0 = 1/u0 in the chapter's notation is effectively the semi-latus rectum a(1 - e^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a classical test, visualized in Figs. 23.3-23.4, derived via the rescaled angle, then applied to Mercury.
prerequisites: angle rescaling for the perturbed orbit
concepts.notes: The identification of r0 with a(1 - e^2) is ours; the book plugs in Mercury's semi-major axis.

concepts.name: anomalous perihelion precession of Mercury
concepts.definition: Mercury's perihelion advances about 575 arcseconds per century; Newtonian perturbations from the other planets account for about 532, solar oblateness for about 0.03, and the residual of about 43 arcseconds per century is explained by general relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 23.6 converts the Schwarzschild formula into numbers and lays out the observational budget; margin note 10 recounts the failed Newtonian fixes and Einstein's reaction.

concepts.name: classical solar-system tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: The historic weak-field checks of GR: perihelion precession of Mercury, deflection of starlight by the Sun, and gravitational redshift; Shapiro radar time delay is often counted as a fourth.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in a shaded margin box when §23.3 begins, with pointers to redshift (Chapter 6) and time delay (Chapter 9).

concepts.name: space and time contributions to perihelion precession
aliases: spatial versus temporal curvature in precession
concepts.definition: To first order, the g_rr (spatial curvature) part of the Schwarzschild metric supplies one third of the perihelion advance and the g_tt (time) part supplies two thirds, so the effect cannot be captured by spatial geometry alone.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated qualitatively at the end of §23.3 (curved space leaves too little path length to close the orbit; the larger share comes from the time part), then quantified in Exercises 23.5 (spatial slice, delta about 2 pi M/r) and 23.6 (flat-space metric with curved g_tt, two thirds of the total).
concepts.notes: The split depends on the coordinates used; the invariant statement is the total 6 pi M/r0.

concepts.name: Flamm's paraboloid
aliases: embedding of the Schwarzschild spatial slice
concepts.definition: The surface in flat 3D Euclidean space whose intrinsic geometry matches the t = const, theta = pi/2 slice of Schwarzschild spacetime, dl^2 = dr^2/(1 - 2M/r) + r^2 dphi^2; in cylindrical coordinates z^2 = 8M(r - 2M).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears in Exercise 23.5 with a hint pointing to Appendix D; approximated locally by a tangent cone to show why a circle of circumference 2 pi r has a longer apparent flat-space radius.
concepts.notes: The exercise text says 'flat spacetime'; it means flat Euclidean 3-space.

concepts.name: rubber-sheet model
concepts.definition: The popular picture of gravity as a mass denting a stretched sheet; at best it represents curvature of a spatial slice and omits the time-time part of the metric, which dominates for slow particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Criticized in margin note 11 after the precession interpretation, with the promise that the exercises examine the point.
prerequisites: space and time contributions to perihelion precession

concepts.name: proper period of a circular orbit
concepts.definition: The proper time elapsed on the orbiting body's clock during one circular revolution; for a Schwarzschild geodesic it is 2 pi r (r/M - 3)^{1/2}, shorter than the coordinate period 2 pi (r^3/M)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 23.1 asks for it both from the line element with a given coordinate speed and from the conserved quantities.
prerequisites: Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild spacetime
conserved angular momentum per unit mass

concepts.name: numerical integration of the orbit equation
concepts.definition: Stepping eqn 23.15 (or the equivalent u-equation) in phi to trace trajectories, flipping the sign of the square root at periapsis and apoapsis.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as Exercise 23.7 for L-tilde/M = 4.3, the same ratio as one of the labelled curves in Fig. 23.1 (the one with a tall barrier and a shallow well); the captions of Figs. 23.2 and 23.3 state that those trajectories were computed from eqn 23.15.
concepts.notes: Integrating the second-order form d^2u/dphi^2 + u = M/L^2 + 3Mu^2 avoids the sign problem; this tip is ours.

concepts.name: eccentricity
concepts.definition: The dimensionless parameter of a conic orbit u = u0(1 + epsilon cos phi); in the relativistic treatment epsilon is defined through epsilon^2 u0^2 = (M^2/L^2)(E^2 - E0^2), which reduces to the Newtonian eccentricity in the weak-field limit.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 20 in margin note 8 and redefined in Example 23.5 to make the relativistic equation mirror the Newtonian one.
prerequisites: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem

concepts.name: effective potential energy
concepts.definition: In Newtonian central-force motion, U_eff(r) = L^2/(2 m r^2) - GMm/r, the gravitational potential energy plus the centrifugal energy of the angular motion, which governs one-dimensional radial motion.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in margin note 2 as the template the relativistic potential imitates.

concepts.name: angular momentum barrier
concepts.definition: The repulsive L^2/(2r^2) contribution to an effective potential that prevents particles with angular momentum from reaching small r; in Newtonian gravity it grows without bound as r goes to zero, but in Schwarzschild spacetime it is overwhelmed by the -M L^2/r^3 term.
concepts.how_introduced: Used implicitly in the contrast of Example 23.2: Newtonian particles with any angular momentum are always deflected, relativistic ones may not be.

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: Units in which G and c are set to 1, so mass M stands for the length GM/c^2 (about 1.5 km for the Sun) and time is measured in lengths.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout; constants are restored only in Example 23.6 to compute Mercury's shift.

concepts.name: de Sitter spacetime
concepts.definition: Spacetime of a positive cosmological constant with no matter; in flat slicing ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2(dr^2 + r^2 dphi^2 + ...) with a(t) = e^{Ht}.
concepts.how_introduced: Only appears in Exercise 23.2 as a setting for computing the proper period of a prescribed circular motion.

concepts.name: four-acceleration of a non-geodesic world line
aliases: acceleration of a circular world line
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of four-velocity along a world line, a^mu = du^mu/dtau + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha u^beta; it vanishes exactly when the world line is a geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 23.4 asks for it on a world line of fixed r and constant angular speed, and for the condition that makes it zero (the Keplerian angular speed).

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element (margin recap)
key_equations.meaning: The exterior geometry of a spherical mass in which all orbits of the chapter move.
key_equations.symbols: M mass in length units; t, r, theta, phi Schwarzschild coordinates

key_equations.name: Conserved quantities (margin recap)
key_equations.meaning: Energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass, constant along geodesics because the metric is independent of t and phi.

key_equations.name: Theta geodesic equation
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equation for theta; at theta = pi/2 the right side vanishes, so an orbit that starts in the equatorial plane with no polar velocity stays there.

key_equations.name: Radial equation in effective-energy form
key_equations.meaning: Exact Schwarzschild radial motion written as one-dimensional Newtonian energy conservation in proper time.
key_equations.symbols: script E effective energy; V_eff effective potential

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian gravity plus centrifugal barrier plus a new attractive r^-3 term responsible for all novel orbital behaviour.

key_equations.name: Newtonian effective potential energy (margin note 2)
key_equations.meaning: The Chapter 20 template for comparison; divide by m and set G = 1 to match the first two terms of 23.3.
key_equations.symbols: L angular momentum; m particle mass

key_equations.name: Extrema of the effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Radii of the stable (r_+, minimum) and unstable (r_-, maximum) circular orbits; real only for L-tilde/M >= sqrt(12).
key_equations.symbols: r_+ outer minimum; r_- inner maximum

key_equations.name: Threshold values of L-tilde/M
key_equations.meaning: Innermost stable circular orbit at 6M; for L = 4M the barrier top is exactly at zero effective energy, the capture threshold for particles from infinity.

key_equations.name: Energy of a circular orbit
key_equations.meaning: Setting dr/dtau = 0 in 23.2 at the minimum. The printed version writes the first factor with plain r and the second with r_+; both mean the circular-orbit radius. With general r it holds at any radial turning point.

key_equations.name: Squared extremum condition (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Eqn 23.4 rearranged and squared to eliminate the square root. The printed equation has 2M^2 in place of 12M^2, a typographical slip.

key_equations.name: Angular momentum of a circular orbit
key_equations.meaning: Specific angular momentum needed for a circular orbit at radius r_+; it diverges as r approaches 3M.

key_equations.name: Energy of a circular orbit in terms of radius
key_equations.meaning: Energy per unit mass of a circular geodesic; at r = 6M it gives E-tilde^2 = 8/9.

key_equations.name: Ratio L/E for a circular orbit (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Divide 23.7 by 23.8. The printed version has r_+^2, which is dimensionally inconsistent and would spoil 23.11; r_+ is correct.

key_equations.name: Coordinate angular velocity
key_equations.meaning: Angular speed as seen with Schwarzschild coordinate time, built from the conserved quantities.

key_equations.name: Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Circular geodesics obey exactly the Newtonian period-radius relation when t and the areal radius r are used.

key_equations.name: Inverse Schwarzschild metric (margin)
key_equations.meaning: Needed to write u.u = -1 in terms of the lowered components u_t and u_phi.

key_equations.name: Normalization with lowered components
key_equations.meaning: Four-velocity normalization in the equatorial plane; u_t and u_phi are fixed by E-tilde and L-tilde.

key_equations.name: Radial velocity squared
key_equations.meaning: Uses g^{rr}(u_r)^2 = g_{rr}(u^r)^2 for a diagonal metric to isolate the radial speed.

key_equations.name: Radial velocity
key_equations.meaning: Radial proper-time velocity as a function of r for given conserved quantities; equivalent to 23.2-23.3.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild orbit equation
key_equations.meaning: Shape of any equatorial massive-particle geodesic; the basis of Figs. 23.2-23.3 and Exercise 23.7.

key_equations.name: Newtonian orbit equation (margin note 8)
key_equations.meaning: Chapter 20 counterpart of 23.15, for side-by-side comparison.
key_equations.symbols: E Newtonian energy; L angular momentum; m mass

key_equations.name: Newtonian u-equation (margin note 8)
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian orbits in u = 1/r: a circle in the (u, u') plane centred at u0, giving the conic u = u0(1 + epsilon cos theta).

key_equations.name: Orbit equation in u = M/r
key_equations.meaning: Dimensionless form of 23.15; the right side is a cubic polynomial in u.

key_equations.name: Orbit equation around u0
key_equations.meaning: The cubic rewritten as a Newtonian-looking left side plus terms that vanish in the Newtonian limit.
key_equations.symbols: u0 circular-orbit value of u; E0 its energy

key_equations.name: Matching condition for u0
key_equations.meaning: Coefficient matching reproduces the circular-orbit radii of 23.4, so u0 = M/r_+ (or M/r_-).

key_equations.name: Energy of the reference circular orbit
key_equations.meaning: Constant-term matching; identical to 23.5 at u0 = M/r_+. The printed left side drops the tilde.

key_equations.name: Newtonian form plus relativistic corrections
key_equations.meaning: Left side is the Newtonian ellipse equation; the right side holds a leading correction of order u0^3 epsilon^2 and a smaller one of order u0^3 epsilon^3. The printed definition just above 23.21 reads epsilon u0^2, missing the square on epsilon.

key_equations.name: Newtonian solution used as zeroth order
key_equations.meaning: Ellipse with the focus at the origin that the relativistic orbit only slightly perturbs.

key_equations.name: Orbit equation with leading correction (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Keeping only the 6u0(u - u0)^2 correction turns the equation into an oscillator with a slightly reduced frequency. The printed version has '=' where '+' belongs.

key_equations.name: Oscillator in the rescaled angle
key_equations.meaning: Radial motion is exactly periodic with period 2 pi in psi. The book writes du/dpsi, which equals dmu/dpsi.

key_equations.name: Azimuth per radial period
key_equations.meaning: One perihelion-to-perihelion cycle sweeps slightly more than a full turn.

key_equations.name: Perihelion advance per orbit
key_equations.meaning: Fractional excess angle per orbit; the central prediction of the chapter.

key_equations.name: Mercury's perihelion shift
key_equations.meaning: With r0 = 5.8e10 m and M = 2e30 kg, about 2e-4 rad or 41 arcsec per century (43 with r0 replaced by the semi-latus rectum).
key_equations.symbols: M_sun solar mass; r0 orbital radius

key_equations.name: Proper period of a circular orbit (Exercise 23.1)
key_equations.meaning: Orbiting clock's time per revolution, from dphi/dtau = L/r^2 and 23.7.

key_equations.name: Exponentially expanding metric (Exercise 23.2)
key_equations.meaning: Setting for a proper-period calculation in a de Sitter-type geometry.

key_equations.name: Equatorial spatial slice (Exercise 23.5)
key_equations.meaning: Geometry of space alone at fixed t, isolating the g_rr contribution.

key_equations.name: Flamm's paraboloid (Exercise 23.5)
key_equations.meaning: Embedding surface in flat 3-space with the same intrinsic geometry as 23.28 (printed with a +/- sign on the right).

key_equations.name: Spatial-curvature wedge angle (Exercise 23.5)
key_equations.meaning: Angle removed from a flat disc to match the true circumference; one third of the full 6 pi M/r advance.

key_equations.name: Flat-space curved-time metric (Exercise 23.6)
key_equations.meaning: Toy spacetime keeping only the g_tt deformation, used to isolate the time contribution to precession.

key_equations.name: Orbit equation in the toy metric (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Second-order orbit equation for 23.31 with u = 1/r. The printed right side has E-tilde to the first power; differentiating the normalization gives E-tilde squared, consistent with 23.33.

key_equations.name: Circular orbit in the toy metric (Exercise 23.6)
key_equations.meaning: Weak-field expansion of 23.32 for a circular orbit; perturbing about it yields two thirds of the Schwarzschild precession.

figures.label: Fig. 23.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Schwarzschild effective potential curves for a handful of values of L-tilde/M.
figures.visual_description: Axes: vertical V_eff(r) with a zero level marked, horizontal |r|. Four curves, all diving to minus infinity near the axis and creeping up to zero from below at large r. One curve shoots up into a tall narrow peak far above zero before dropping into a shallow well; its label 4.3 is placed beside that well. The curve labelled 4 has a much lower peak whose top just reaches the zero line. The curve labelled sqrt(12) has no separate peak and well, only a flat shoulder (inflection) below zero. The curve labelled 3 climbs monotonically with no extrema.
figures.what_it_teaches: How the shape of V_eff, and hence which orbits exist, is controlled by the single ratio L-tilde/M: a barrier plus well for large ratios, barrier top at zero for 4, merging into an inflection at sqrt(12), and no well below that.

redesign.idea: Live effective-potential explorer: V_eff(r) drawn with the Newtonian potential ghosted behind it, the r^-3 term shaded as the region where they differ, and markers for r_+ and r_- that slide, merge at 6M and vanish.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags an L-tilde/M slider (2 to 8) and a mass-scale toggle; readouts show r_+, r_-, V_eff at each and flag the special values sqrt(12) and 4 with a snap-to option; a checkbox overlays several curves at once to reproduce the book's family.

figures.label: Fig. 23.2(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (a) of the allowed-trajectory figure: a circular orbit sitting at the bottom of the potential well.
figures.visual_description: Left: V_eff(r) against |r| with a zero line; a curve with a sharp peak near the axis and a shallow well below zero, with a black dot at the bottom of the well. Right: a circle with a dot at its centre representing the orbit around the central mass.
figures.what_it_teaches: A particle whose energy equals the minimum of V_eff has fixed r but still circulates; the bound energy is negative.

redesign.idea: Linked potential-and-orbit view: a draggable energy line on V_eff drives a live orbit integration in a side panel.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the energy level to the well minimum and sees the orbit become a circle; nudging slightly above produces a small-amplitude rosette whose precession rate is displayed.

figures.label: Fig. 23.2(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (b): an unbound particle reflected by the potential barrier.
figures.visual_description: Left: the same V_eff curve with a horizontal energy line above zero extending from large r inward until it meets the right flank of the tall peak. Right: a trajectory that enters from the upper right, swings round a central dot in a tight hook or loop, and heads back out.
figures.what_it_teaches: When the energy line hits the barrier, the particle has a turning point and escapes again; strong-field scattering can wrap the path around the centre by a large angle, unlike a gentle Newtonian hyperbola.

redesign.idea: Impact-parameter shooting gallery: particles launched from the right at a chosen speed and impact parameter, colour coded by outcome (scattered or captured), with the deflection angle plotted.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets the incoming energy and L-tilde (or impact parameter) and fires a fan of trajectories; a companion V_eff plot shows each energy line relative to the barrier top.

figures.label: Fig. 23.2(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (c): a higher-energy particle that clears the barrier and spirals inward.
figures.visual_description: Left: V_eff curve with a horizontal energy line drawn above the top of the peak, so it never meets the curve. Right: a spiral curling inward toward a central dot, like a snail shell.
figures.what_it_teaches: If the effective energy exceeds the barrier maximum there is no inner turning point, so the particle is captured, something impossible in Newtonian gravity with nonzero angular momentum.
concepts: relativistic r^-3 term in the effective potential

redesign.idea: Newton-versus-Schwarzschild split screen: the same launch conditions integrated in both theories, Newtonian orbit bouncing off its infinite wall while the relativistic one spirals in.
redesign.interaction: Learner raises the energy slider through the barrier height and watches the right-hand orbit switch from scattering to capture while the Newtonian one never does; a marker shows the barrier height updating with L-tilde.

figures.label: Fig. 23.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bound precessing orbit: the particle bounces between two radii in the potential and the orbit rotates (precession much exaggerated).
figures.visual_description: Left: V_eff against |r| with a tall narrow peak near the axis and a shallow well below zero; a short horizontal energy line sits inside the well, below the zero level, with dots where it meets the curve on either side (the periapsis and apoapsis radii). Right: three overlapping near-elliptical loops around a central dot, forming a rosette, enclosed by a single dotted circle marking the outer turning radius; the inner turning radius is visible only as the small empty region the loops leave around the centre.
figures.what_it_teaches: Radial oscillation between periapsis and apoapsis plus an azimuthal advance of more than 2 pi per radial cycle produce a rotating near-ellipse.

redesign.idea: Rosette builder with a precession dial: orbit traced in real time with the dotted periapsis and apoapsis circles, a trail that fades, and a counter of degrees advanced per radial period compared with the formula 6 pi M/r0.
redesign.interaction: Learner chooses M/r0 (from Mercury-like 1e-8 up to 0.15) and eccentricity; a magnify control exaggerates tiny precession for visibility; toggles show the Newtonian closed ellipse for reference and pause at each perihelion.

figures.label: Fig. 23.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Geometry of the perihelion advance: successive near-ellipses rotated about the focus by an angle delta phi.
figures.visual_description: About nine overlapping ellipses of the same shape share a focus marked by a black dot near the left; each is rotated slightly anticlockwise relative to the previous one, so their far ends fan out to the right. Two straight lines leave the focus: one horizontal to the far point of the first ellipse and one tilted to the far point of a later ellipse, with the angle between them labelled delta phi; a short dotted arc curls around the focus where all the perihelia crowd together.
figures.what_it_teaches: Precession is a steady rotation of the orbit's major axis by a fixed angle per orbit.

redesign.idea: Time-lapse of the apsidal line: an orbit animation that leaves a ghost ellipse each revolution and draws the rotating major axis, with the accumulated angle compared to Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century scale.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets the number of orbits and the exaggeration factor; hovering a ghost ellipse shows its orbit number and cumulative delta phi; a 'real Mercury' button shows how many centuries a visible rotation would take.

figures.label: Fig. 23.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: (a) A cone tangent to the embedding surface, comparing the slant radius R with the true circle radius R cos alpha; (b) cutting a wedge of angle delta from a flat disc of radius R so its rim matches the shorter circumference.
figures.visual_description: (a) Vertical z axis and horizontal r axis; two curves open upward like a funnel cross-section, with straight lines forming a V (the tangent cone) from a point on the z axis. A horizontal line at the top spans to the cone, labelled R cos alpha, and a slanted segment from the apex labelled R, with the small angle alpha marked between them. (b) Two concentric circles forming a ring, with a narrow wedge at the top bounded by two radii and marked delta by a double-headed arrow, and a radius arrow labelled R.
figures.what_it_teaches: On a curved spatial slice an orbit of circumference 2 pi r lies at a larger distance from the centre than flat geometry suggests; flattening the local cone requires removing a wedge, and this angular deficit contributes part of the perihelion advance.
concepts: space and time contributions to perihelion precession

redesign.idea: 3D paper-cone lab: a rotatable Flamm paraboloid with a tangent cone at the orbit radius that can be unrolled into a flat sector, showing the missing wedge delta; a bar chart splits the total precession into the one-third spatial and two-thirds temporal shares.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the orbit radius r and M; the cone and its unrolled sector update, delta = 2 pi M/r is displayed, and an ellipse drawn on the cone precesses when unrolled; a toggle switches on the g_tt contribution to reach the full 6 pi M/r.

worked_examples.label: Example 23.1
worked_examples.problem: Justify restricting Schwarzschild orbits to the equatorial plane.
worked_examples.method: Vary the line element with respect to theta to get the theta geodesic equation, note that theta = pi/2 makes its source term vanish, so r^2 dtheta/dtau keeps its initial zero value; rotate coordinates so any orbit starts this way and use conservation of L-tilde along the whole geodesic.
worked_examples.key_insight: Spherical symmetry lets us choose the orbital plane as the equator; planarity is the relativistic shadow of angular momentum conservation.
worked_examples.result: theta = pi/2 and dL-tilde/dtau = 0 for all proper time.
concepts: conserved angular momentum per unit mass

worked_examples.label: Example 23.2
worked_examples.problem: Interpret three sample trajectories computed for one choice of M and nonzero L-tilde in terms of the effective potential.
worked_examples.method: Overlay the particle's effective energy on V_eff: at the well minimum the orbit is circular; an energy line above zero that hits the barrier gives a scattering orbit; an energy line above the barrier top gives a capture spiral. Compare with the Newtonian potential whose centrifugal wall is infinite.
worked_examples.key_insight: Where the energy line meets V_eff only the radial velocity vanishes; the finite barrier height is what allows relativistic capture of particles with angular momentum.
worked_examples.result: Three orbit classes: circular (negative energy), scattered (positive energy below peak), captured (energy above peak).

worked_examples.label: Example 23.3
worked_examples.problem: Find the energy, angular momentum and their ratio for a circular geodesic of radius r_+.
worked_examples.method: Set dr/dtau = 0 so E = V_eff(r_+), giving E-tilde^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2); square the extremum condition 23.4 and rearrange to L^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M); substitute to get E-tilde^2, then divide to get (L/E)^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Circular orbits need infinite angular momentum as r approaches 3M, and the L/E ratio is exactly what is needed for the coordinate angular velocity.
worked_examples.result: L^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M); E^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(r - 2M)/(r - 3M); (L/E)^2 = M r (1 - 2M/r)^{-2} (printed with r^2 and 2M^2 slips in 23.9 and 23.6).
concepts: energy and angular momentum of circular Schwarzschild orbits

worked_examples.problem: Show that Kepler's third law for circular orbits survives in Schwarzschild spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Write dphi/dt as (dphi/dtau)/(dt/dtau) using L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dtau and E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau, then insert (L/E)^2 from Example 23.3.
worked_examples.key_insight: All relativistic factors cancel when time is Schwarzschild coordinate time.
concepts: Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild spacetime

worked_examples.label: Example 23.4
worked_examples.problem: Describe qualitatively a bound orbit whose energy lies inside the potential well.
worked_examples.method: Mark the two intersections of the energy line with V_eff as the minimum and maximum radii and follow the particle oscillating between them while phi advances (Fig. 23.3).
worked_examples.key_insight: Bound Schwarzschild orbits are rosettes: near-ellipses whose axes rotate.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the equation for the shape r(phi) of an equatorial orbit without solving the second-order geodesic equations.
worked_examples.method: Write u.u = -1 with inverse metric components and lowered u_t, u_phi fixed by E-tilde and L-tilde; use g^{rr}(u_r)^2 = g_{rr}(u^r)^2 to isolate (dr/dtau)^2; take the root and divide by dphi/dtau = L/r^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two conserved quantities plus normalization give a complete first-order description; the orbit shape is just the ratio of two proper-time rates.

worked_examples.label: Example 23.5
worked_examples.problem: Recast the Schwarzschild orbit equation so that it looks like the Newtonian ellipse equation plus small corrections.
worked_examples.method: Substitute u = M/r to get a cubic for (du/dphi)^2; posit the form Newtonian circle-offset + 6u0(u - u0)^2 + 2(u - u0)^3 + constant; match powers of u to fix u0 (reproducing the circular-orbit radii) and E0; define epsilon via the leftover constant; estimate the correction sizes as u0^3 epsilon^2 and u0^3 epsilon^3.
worked_examples.key_insight: Relativity adds a quadratic term that changes the oscillation frequency and a cubic term that is smaller by a factor of epsilon; the quadratic one is what drives precession.
concepts: near-Newtonian expansion of the orbit equation

worked_examples.problem: Solve the leading-order perturbed orbit equation and extract the perihelion advance.
worked_examples.method: Keep (u')^2 + (1 - 6u0)(u - u0)^2 = u0^2 epsilon^2; define psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi and mu = u - u0 to obtain a harmonic oscillator of period 2 pi in psi; convert back to phi and expand the square root to first order in M/r0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Precession is a frequency mismatch: the radial oscillation is slightly slower than the azimuthal rotation, so perihelion returns after more than 2 pi.
worked_examples.result: Delta phi = 2 pi (1 - 6M/r0)^{-1/2} ~ 2 pi (1 + 3M/r0); delta phi = 6 pi M/r0 per orbit.
concepts: angle rescaling for the perturbed orbit

worked_examples.label: Example 23.6
worked_examples.problem: Estimate Mercury's relativistic perihelion shift and compare with observation.
worked_examples.method: Restore G and c in 6 pi M/r0, insert M = 2e30 kg and r0 = 5.8e10 m, multiply by the number of 88-day orbits per century and convert radians to arcseconds; then set against the measured total precession and its Newtonian contributions.
worked_examples.key_insight: A tiny fractional effect (GM/c^2 r of order 1e-8) accumulates to a measurable 43 arcseconds per century that Newtonian models could not explain.
worked_examples.result: About 4.8e-7 rad per orbit, 2e-4 rad or 41 arcsec per century; refined GR value 43.0; observed residual 43.1 +/- 0.5 out of about 575 total.

worked_examples.problem: Find the special angular momenta at which the potential changes character.
worked_examples.method: Use eqn 23.4: the square root vanishes at L/M = sqrt(12), giving a single inflection at 6M; for L/M = 4 evaluate r_- = 4M and check V_eff(4M) = -1/4 + 1/2 - 1/4 = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: One dimensionless number decides whether stable orbits exist and whether particles from infinity can be turned back.
worked_examples.result: ISCO at 6M for L/M = sqrt(12); zero-height barrier at 4M for L/M = 4.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A bead rolling along a one-dimensional hill-and-valley track (the effective potential) with an energy line as its water level
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The radial motion is literally one-dimensional energy conservation, so circular orbits are the valley floor, turning points are where the level meets the track, and capture happens when the level tops the hill.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The bead picture hides the phi motion (the particle moves even at a turning point, which the book stresses) and the fact that script E is not a real kinetic plus potential energy; it also only describes proper-time dynamics.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split view with a bead on the V_eff track and the actual orbit, synchronized in proper time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Newtonian centrifugal wall versus a finite hill with a pit behind it
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: relativistic r^-3 term in the effective potential
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: In Newtonian gravity any angular momentum builds an infinitely tall wall near the centre; the extra relativistic term caps the wall at a finite height, so a fast enough particle rolls over it into the pit.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Height and position of the hill depend on L-tilde, so the picture must be redrawn for each particle.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph animation from the Newtonian to the Schwarzschild potential as a 'relativity dial' turns on the r^-3 term.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A Spirograph rosette: an ellipse that is slowly rotated each time it is drawn
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Figs. 23.3 and 23.4 show near-ellipses whose axes turn, letting learners see precession as rotation of a familiar shape.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The real orbit is a single continuous curve, not a sequence of closed ellipses; the ellipse is only an osculating approximation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draw the true orbit and, on demand, the osculating ellipse at each perihelion passage.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Two clocks that tick at slightly different rates: the radial oscillation and the angular sweep
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: angle rescaling for the perturbed orbit
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The substitution psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi says the radial motion completes a cycle at 2 pi in psi, i.e. a little after 2 pi in phi; the mismatch accumulates as precession.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Our framing of the book's rescaling; it works cleanly only at linear order in the eccentricity-sized perturbation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two dials, one for phi and one for radial phase, rotating side by side; their lag angle after each radial cycle is the precession.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Making a cone from a paper disc by cutting out a wedge
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: space and time contributions to perihelion precession
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Exercise 23.5 approximates the curved spatial slice by a tangent cone; a flat-looking circle of radius R has too much circumference, so a wedge delta must be removed, and an orbit laid on the cone advances by that wedge each turn.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Captures only the spatial third of the effect and only approximately (the paraboloid is not a cone).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Paper-cone cutter: unroll the tangent cone to a sector, draw an ellipse, roll it back up and watch the perihelion move.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Not enough path length to close the orbit
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Spatial curvature makes the path around the centre shorter than flat intuition predicts, so the particle 'runs out of room' and overshoots the Newtonian closing point.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The authors immediately add that the larger part comes from the time part of the metric, so this intuition alone gives the wrong magnitude (one third).

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Invoked negatively: a stretched-sheet picture depicts only spatial curvature and misses the half of the story that controls slow particles.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Actively misleading for orbital precession and for why things fall at all.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between a 'space only' and 'space plus time' simulation of Mercury to show the sheet gives one third of the precession.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: At a point where the energy line meets V_eff the particle is momentarily at rest.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the radial velocity is zero there; with nonzero L-tilde the particle keeps moving in phi.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In the one-dimensional bead picture a turning point means zero speed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A particle with any angular momentum can never fall straight into the central mass.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Schwarzschild spacetime the centrifugal barrier has finite height; particles with energy above the peak spiral in, and for L-tilde < 4M no particle from infinity is turned back.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian intuition: the L^2/r^2 barrier grows without limit at small r.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Stable circular orbits exist at every radius outside the central object, just as in Newtonian gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: No stable circular orbit exists inside r = 6M; between 3M and 6M circular orbits are unstable and inside 3M none exist.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian circular orbits exist at every radius, and the potential looks Newtonian far away.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: General relativity must modify Kepler's third law for circular orbits.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Using Schwarzschild coordinate time and the areal radius, (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^3 exactly. The orbiting clock's proper period does differ.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Relativity changes most orbital formulas, so the learner expects correction factors here too.
concepts: Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild spacetime
proper period of a circular orbit

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Assuming the orbit lies in the equatorial plane is a special case that loses generality.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Spherical symmetry lets coordinates be rotated so any orbit starts equatorially, and the theta equation keeps it there.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Setting theta = pi/2 looks like an arbitrary simplifying choice.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All of Mercury's roughly 575 arcsec per century perihelion advance is a relativistic effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: About 532 arcsec per century comes from other planets and a tiny amount from solar oblateness; only the residual 43 arcsec per century is relativistic.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts mention Mercury's precession as proof of GR without the budget.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Perihelion precession is caused by the curvature of space, as a rubber-sheet picture suggests.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Spatial curvature gives only about a third of the advance; the larger part comes from the time-time part of the metric.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Visualizations of curved space are ubiquitous and time curvature is hard to picture.
concepts: space and time contributions to perihelion precession

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The variable u = 1/r (or M/r) is a component of the four-velocity u.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is an unrelated inverse-radius variable borrowed from Chapter 20 that happens to share the letter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both appear in the same derivation within a few lines.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The maximum of the effective potential is irrelevant because nothing can sit there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a genuine but unstable circular orbit; its photon analogue (at 3M) matters in the next chapter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Only minima are usually associated with orbits.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The gap between the chapter's 41 arcsec and the accepted 43 arcsec per century reflects subtle higher-order GR physics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Almost all of it comes from inserting the semi-major axis for r0. In the derivation r0 = 1/u0 plays the role of the semi-latus rectum a(1 - e^2); for Mercury (e about 0.21) that length, with the accurate solar mass, raises the leading-order estimate to about 43.0 (about 43.2 if the book's rounded 2e30 kg is kept).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book attributes the refined value to less severe approximations without saying which.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Schwarzschild r is the physical distance from the centre, so the orbit radius is just r.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: r is defined by circumference 2 pi r; proper radial distance is larger, which is exactly the geometric fact exploited in Exercise 23.5.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The letter r and the Newtonian-looking formulas invite a flat-space reading.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Precession only works for nearly circular orbits because the derivation assumed small eccentricity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: To first order in M/r0 the advance 6 pi M/[a(1 - e^2)] holds for any eccentricity; the dropped cubic term affects orbit shape and only shifts the frequency at second order in M/r0.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter justifies dropping the cubic term by appealing to small epsilon.
concepts: near-Newtonian expansion of the orbit equation

thought_experiments.name: Throwing test particles in from infinity
thought_experiments.setup: Send particles toward a Schwarzschild mass with the same angular momentum but increasing energy, or the same energy but decreasing angular momentum.
thought_experiments.lesson: Below the barrier top they scatter; above it they are captured; for L-tilde below 4M nothing arriving from infinity comes back.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Capture cross-section map: a 2D grid over (energy, L-tilde) coloured by fate, with a click launching the corresponding trajectory.

thought_experiments.name: Lowering a circular orbit toward the mass
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine a satellite on ever smaller circular orbits, reading off the required L-tilde and E-tilde at each radius from Example 23.3.
thought_experiments.lesson: The required angular momentum has a minimum at 6M and blows up at 3M; below 6M the orbits become unstable, so gradual inspiral ends in a plunge.
concepts: energy and angular momentum of circular Schwarzschild orbits
thought_experiments.app_idea: Plot L-tilde(r) and E-tilde(r) for circular orbits with a draggable radius marker and a stability colour band.

thought_experiments.name: Space-only and time-only Schwarzschild worlds
thought_experiments.setup: Build two artificial geometries: one keeping only the curved spatial slice (Exercise 23.5) and one keeping only the modified g_tt with flat space (Exercise 23.6), and compute orbital precession in each.
thought_experiments.lesson: Space curvature alone gives about one third of the advance and time curvature about two thirds, so gravity is not just bent space.
concepts: space and time contributions to perihelion precession
thought_experiments.app_idea: Three-column orbit simulator (space-only, time-only, full Schwarzschild) sharing initial conditions, with precession readouts adding up.

thought_experiments.name: Unrolling the tangent cone
thought_experiments.setup: Lay a circular orbit on the cone tangent to Flamm's paraboloid and unroll the cone onto a flat table.
thought_experiments.lesson: The unrolled circle is missing a wedge of angle about 2 pi M/r, so a closed flat ellipse drawn across the gap reappears rotated.
concepts: space and time contributions to perihelion precession
thought_experiments.app_idea: Physical-feel 3D cone with a cut seam that the learner drags open and closed.

historical_notes.event: Elliptical planetary orbits and their Newtonian explanation, recalled as the benchmark GR had to improve on.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the chapter: GR's early success was matching observations more closely than Kepler-Newton ellipses.

historical_notes.event: An unexplained residual in Mercury's perihelion advance was known from the 1850s; proposed Newtonian fixes included raising Venus's mass by about ten percent or postulating an unseen swarm of asteroids near Mercury.
historical_notes.significance: Shows the anomaly was robust against ad hoc Newtonian repairs, which made GR's parameter-free explanation compelling. (The book does not name Le Verrier, who first reported it in 1859.)

historical_notes.event: Einstein's calculation of Mercury's perihelion shift matched the unexplained residual; as related in Pais's biography, he wrote to Ehrenfest of days of joyful excitement and described palpitations and a feeling that something snapped inside him.
historical_notes.significance: The first quantitative success of general relativity and a powerful personal confirmation for Einstein. (Year supplied by us; the book gives none.)

historical_notes.event: Flamm's paraboloid, the embedding of the Schwarzschild spatial slice, is named after him in Exercise 23.5 (life dates 1885-1964 given).
historical_notes.significance: Earliest visualization of Schwarzschild spatial geometry, used here to isolate spatial curvature's share of precession. (He published it in 1916.)

historical_notes.event: Chapter epigraph: Hobbes's reputed last words about a final voyage and a leap in the dark.
historical_notes.significance: Playful nod to orbits that plunge into the dark centre, anticipating capture orbits and black holes.

applications_and_observations.details: Restoring constants, 6 pi GM/(c^2 r0) with the book's inputs gives about 4.8e-7 rad per orbit; with about 415 orbits per century that is about 2e-4 rad or 41 arcsec per century. A careful GR treatment gives 43.0. Our check: replacing r0 by Mercury's semi-latus rectum a(1 - e^2) = 5.55e10 m gives 43.0 arcsec per century with GM_sun = 1.327e20 m^3 s^-2 (about 43.2 with the book's rounded M = 2e30 kg).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Period 88 d (7.6e6 s); r0 = 5.8e10 m; M_sun = 2e30 kg; 4.8e-7 rad/orbit; ~41 arcsec/century (book), 43.0 (refined); with a(1-e^2) = 5.55e10 m, 43.0-43.2 depending on the solar mass used (our estimate).

applications_and_observations.details: Observed total advance compared with Newtonian perturbations from the other planets, the Sun's oblateness and the relativistic residual.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Total ~575 arcsec/century; planets ~532; solar oblateness ~0.03; residual observed 43.1 +/- 0.5; GR 43.0.

applications_and_observations.details: Perihelion precession of Mercury, light bending by the Sun and gravitational redshift, plus Shapiro time delay as a fourth test.

applications_and_observations.topic: Innermost stable circular orbit and accretion efficiency (our extension)
applications_and_observations.details: Not discussed in the chapter, but follows directly from eqns 23.4 and 23.8: gas in an accretion disc around a non-rotating black hole spirals through circular orbits down to 6M and then plunges, radiating the binding energy 1 - E-tilde(6M).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: r_ISCO = 6GM/c^2 (about 89 km for 10 solar masses); E-tilde(6M) = sqrt(8/9) = 0.943, so about 5.7 percent of rest-mass energy released (our computation).

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the relativistic correction in the solar system
applications_and_observations.details: The dimensionless parameter controlling precession is GM/(c^2 r0), which for Mercury is about 2.6e-8, explaining why the effect is tiny per orbit but accumulates over centuries (our estimate from the book's numbers).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: GM_sun/c^2 ~ 1.5 km; GM_sun/(c^2 r0) ~ 2.6e-8 for Mercury.

applications_and_observations.details: Figures 23.2-23.3 were generated by integrating eqn 23.15, and Exercise 23.7 asks readers to write such a program for L-tilde/M = 4.3, handling the change of sign at turning points.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: For L-tilde/M = 4.3: r_+ ~ 14.7M, r_- ~ 3.77M, V_eff(r_+) ~ -0.031, V_eff(r_-) ~ +0.040 (our computation).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometric units G = c = 1 throughout; M denotes GM/c^2. Constants are restored only in Example 23.6.
E-tilde and L-tilde are energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass; E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r)u^t, L-tilde = r^2 sin^2 theta u^phi (r^2 u^phi in the equatorial plane).
Script E = (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2, with V_eff per unit mass; contrasted with the Newtonian U_eff that carries the particle mass m.
r_+ is the outer extremum (minimum, stable circular orbit) and r_- the inner one (maximum, unstable), from the +/- sign in eqn 23.4.
Figures label the vertical axis V_eff(r-vector) and the horizontal axis |r-vector|, a Newtonian-style notation for the Schwarzschild radial coordinate.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In GR there is no position vector; read it as the areal coordinate r.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Bold u is the four-velocity; plain u = 1/r in the Newtonian margin note, and u = M/r (dimensionless) from Example 23.5 on; primes denote d/dphi.
u0 = M/r0 is the circular-orbit value of u about which the orbit is expanded, E-tilde_0 its energy, epsilon defined by epsilon^2 u0^2 = (M/L)^2 (E^2 - E0^2).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Printed text sometimes drops the tilde (E0) and the square on epsilon.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Delta phi is the azimuth swept between successive perihelia; delta phi = Delta phi - 2 pi is the advance per orbit.
psi = (1 - 6u0)^{1/2} phi and mu = u - u0.
