notable.summary: For a circular orbit, find the proper period first from the line element with a given coordinate speed, then from the conserved quantities, and check the two agree with the closed form 2 pi r (r/M - 3)^{1/2}.
notable.why_notable: Connects Example 23.3 and Kepler's law to what an orbiting clock actually records.

notable.summary: A world line at fixed radius with uniform angular rate is prescribed; fix its time-dilation constant from normalization, compute the four-acceleration, and find when it vanishes.
notable.why_notable: Recovers circular geodesics (and Kepler's law) from the acceleration side instead of the potential side.

notable.summary: Embed the equatorial spatial slice as Flamm's paraboloid, approximate it by a tangent cone, show the circumference mismatch requires removing a wedge of about 2 pi M/r, argue this advances an elliptical orbit's perihelion by that amount, and compare with the full shift.
notable.why_notable: Isolates the spatial-curvature third of the precession with a tactile geometric picture.

notable.summary: In a toy spacetime with flat space but Schwarzschild g_tt, derive dr/dphi from normalization, obtain a second-order equation for u = 1/r, find the circular orbit in the weak-field limit, perturb about it, and show the precession is two thirds of the Schwarzschild value. The hint steers learners to a harmonic-oscillator equation for the perturbation with frequency omega_0 and to locating successive closest approaches where omega_0 phi is a multiple of 2 pi.
notable.why_notable: Quantifies the chapter's claim that time curvature dominates, and teaches the standard oscillator method for precession. Note the printed eqn 23.32 needs E-tilde squared.

notable.summary: Write a program that integrates eqn 23.15 for L-tilde/M = 4.3, choosing the root sign according to whether the particle is approaching or receding from periapsis.
notable.why_notable: Turns the chapter into a hands-on lab and reproduces the book's figures.

notable.summary: Compute the proper time for one circuit of uniform circular motion in a flat, exponentially expanding metric with a specified velocity definition.
notable.why_notable: Transfers the proper-period calculation to a cosmological geometry from Part III.

notable.summary: Find how Schwarzschild time t relates to proper time for a particle held at constant radius.
notable.why_notable: Quick reminder that the g_tt factor alone controls static clocks, setting up the time-curvature argument.

exercises.solutions: Some answers may appear in GA Appendix E (Answers to selected problems); Blennow and Ohlsson contain solved harder variants of 23.1-23.4.

difficulty.notes: The effective-potential half (§23.1-23.2) is gentle and graphical for anyone who has done Chapter 20. The perihelion derivation in Example 23.5 compresses a completing-the-square and coefficient-matching step into 'massaged', and several printed slips (2M^2 for 12M^2 in 23.6, r_+^2 for r_+ in 23.9, epsilon for epsilon^2 before 23.21, '=' for '+' in 23.22, E-tilde for E-tilde^2 in 23.32) will stall careful readers. The physical interpretation (space versus time curvature) is only hinted at in the text and needs the two harder exercises.

teaching_gems.gem: Write the relativistic radial equation so it is visually identical to the Newtonian one and point to a single extra term (-M L^2/r^3) as the source of every new orbital phenomenon.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners reuse all their Chapter 20 intuition and focus attention on one small, nameable difference.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A 'relativity dial' that scales the r^-3 term from 0 to 1, morphing the potential and the orbit simultaneously.

teaching_gems.gem: Pair each potential plot with its energy line and the orbit it produces (circular, scattered, captured, precessing).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects an abstract 1D graph to a 2D trajectory and makes orbit classification a visual reading task.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable energy line on V_eff with a synchronized orbit integrator and a bead moving on the potential curve.

teaching_gems.gem: Reduce the zoo of orbit types to two magic numbers of L-tilde/M: sqrt(12) (no stable orbits below, ISCO at 6M) and 4 (barrier top at zero, capture threshold).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Memorable anchors that organize the phase space and can be checked with one line of algebra.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Slider with snap points at sqrt(12) and 4 that trigger short narrated explanations and highlight the potential's shape change.

teaching_gems.gem: Show that Kepler's third law is unchanged in Schwarzschild coordinate time.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A surprising null result that doubles as a strong algebra check and prompts a discussion of which time is being used.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Circular-orbit panel showing coordinate period, proper period and Newtonian period side by side as radius shrinks toward 6M.

teaching_gems.gem: Get the orbit shape from normalization plus conserved quantities, dividing dr/dtau by dphi/dtau, avoiding second-order geodesic equations.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Short, reusable recipe that works for any metric with two Killing symmetries (and is reused for photons).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation card deck where each step highlights which symmetry or identity is used.

teaching_gems.gem: Rescale the angle so the perturbed orbit is an exact oscillator; precession becomes the mismatch between 2 pi in psi and 2 pi in phi.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns a messy perturbation problem into a one-line frequency argument that generalizes to any near-circular precession.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two rotating phase dials (radial phase and azimuth) whose growing offset traces the rotating apsidal line.

teaching_gems.gem: Give the full Mercury bookkeeping (575 total, 532 planets, 0.03 oblateness, 43 residual) with the story of failed Newtonian patches.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows how a small but stubborn residual becomes decisive evidence, and teaches scientific skepticism about the headline number.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stacked bar or waterfall chart of precession contributions with hover cards for each historical hypothesis.

teaching_gems.gem: Split precession into spatial (cone wedge, one third) and temporal (g_tt only toy metric, two thirds) contributions through deliberately artificial geometries.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Directly refutes the rubber-sheet picture with a calculation the learner can do, making time curvature tangible.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three synchronized simulators (space-only, time-only, full) whose precession readouts sum to the Schwarzschild value.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 23.6 has (1 - 2M^2/L^2) where squaring eqn 23.4 gives (1 - 12M^2/L^2).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader checking the algebra cannot reproduce 23.7 and may doubt the result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the corrected relation and derive L^2/r^2 = M/(r - 3M) directly by eliminating between dV/dr = 0 and E = V_eff.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 23.9 gives (L/E)^2 = M r_+^2 (1 - 2M/r_+)^{-2}; the correct power is r_+ to the first.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Substituting the printed form into 23.10 gives (dphi/dt)^2 = M/r^2, not the Kepler result, and is dimensionally wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected formula and include a dimensional check as a habit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Just before eqn 23.21 the definition is printed as epsilon u0^2 rather than epsilon^2 u0^2; eqn 23.20 writes E0 without the tilde.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether epsilon is an eccentricity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define epsilon^2 u0^2 = (M/L)^2 (E^2 - E0^2) explicitly and show it reduces to Newtonian eccentricity.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 23.22 reads (u')^2 = (1 - 6u0)(u - u0)^2 = u0^2 epsilon^2; the first '=' should be '+'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The equation as printed is inconsistent and the oscillator structure is obscured.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write (u')^2 + (1 - 6u0)(u - u0)^2 = u0^2 epsilon^2 and point out it is an ellipse in the (u - u0, u') plane.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise eqn 23.32 has E-tilde on the right; differentiating the normalization condition gives E-tilde squared, as the following eqn 23.33 assumes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students attempting Exercise 23.6 will not reach the printed target.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Flag the correction in any assignment based on this exercise.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The step from 23.17 to 23.18 is described only as massaging; the completing-the-square and coefficient matching are left to the reader, and it is not stated that u0 is the relativistic circular-orbit value rather than the Newtonian u0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may think the Newtonian u0 = M/L^2 is intended and get lost in the matching.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the expansion explicitly or use the second-order form u'' + u = M/L^2 + 3M u^2 (in u = 1/r) and linearize about the circular orbit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: r0 is plugged in as Mercury's orbital radius (5.8e10 m, the semi-major axis) although in the derivation it is effectively the semi-latus rectum a(1 - e^2); the 41 versus 43 arcsec discrepancy is attributed vaguely to cruder approximations.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners do not see that the leading-order formula already gives 43 arcsec when the correct length is used.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach delta phi = 6 pi GM/[c^2 a(1 - e^2)] and have learners compute 43.0 arcsec per century.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Dropping 2(u - u0)^3 is justified by small eccentricity, but the first-order precession is independent of eccentricity; the cubic term only affects the frequency at second order in M/r0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Creates the false impression that the prediction fails for eccentric orbits such as binary pulsars.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention that 6 pi M/[a(1 - e^2)] holds for any e to first order in M/a, and optionally show the Lindstedt argument.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book calls the extrema of V_eff 'turning points', a term usually reserved for radii where the energy line meets V_eff.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mixes up circular-orbit radii with periapsis/apoapsis radii.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use 'extrema' or 'circular-orbit radii' for V_eff' = 0 and 'turning points' for E = V_eff.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The L-tilde = 4M capture statement is really about marginally unbound particles (effective energy just above zero); more energetic incoming particles need larger L-tilde to avoid capture.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: May conclude that any particle with L-tilde > 4M is safe.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the capture region in the (E, L) plane rather than a single threshold.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Kepler's third law is said to be unaltered without stressing that this holds in Schwarzschild coordinate time and areal radius, not in proper time or proper distance.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may overgeneralize to 'GR does not change orbital periods'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair the result with Exercise 23.1 (proper period) and note what a distant observer versus the orbiter measures.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The space-versus-time interpretation of precession is asserted in one paragraph and demonstrated only in exercises, whose one-third/two-thirds split is coordinate dependent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key conceptual payoff may be skipped, or taken as an invariant fact.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Do the two toy-metric calculations in the main teaching flow and add a caveat that the split refers to Schwarzschild coordinates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 23.2 imagines captured particles crashing into the star, without discussing that neutron stars or black holes can be compact enough for capture to matter, while ordinary stars are far larger than 6M.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Unclear when ISCO and capture are physically relevant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Compare the Sun's radius (about 470000 M_sun-lengths) with 6M and point forward to black holes and accretion discs.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'In Newtonian gravity, can a comet with even a little sideways motion ever hit the exact centre of a point-mass Sun?' Use the answer (no, the centrifugal barrier is infinite) as the hook for what relativity changes.

Check prerequisites fast: can the learner sketch the Newtonian effective potential and read orbits off an energy line? Do they know E-tilde and L-tilde from Chapter 22? If not, spend a few minutes on Chapter 20 §20.3 before starting.

Recommended order: planar motion (Example 23.1) -> V_eff and its r^-3 term -> extrema and the two magic numbers sqrt(12) and 4 -> orbit classes with energy lines -> circular-orbit relations and Kepler's law -> orbit equation from u.u = -1 -> near-Newtonian expansion -> angle rescaling and 6 pi M/r0 -> Mercury numbers -> space versus time split.
When presenting eqns 23.6, 23.9, 23.21, 23.22 and 23.32, use the corrected versions and, if the learner is reading the book, tell them about the printed slips up front to prevent frustration.

Check for understanding: ask the learner to predict what happens to a particle with L-tilde/M = 3.8 coming in from infinity with a small positive energy (captured, since L < 4M), and one with L-tilde/M = 5 and the same energy (scattered).
Check for understanding: 'Why is there no stable circular orbit at r = 5M?' Expected answer: at 5M the extremum is a maximum, since stable minima only exist beyond 6M.

Common question: 'Does GR really leave Kepler's third law unchanged?' Answer: yes in Schwarzschild coordinate time with the areal radius; an orbiting clock measures a shorter period, 2 pi r (r/M - 3)^{1/2}.

Common question: 'Why does the orbit precess forward rather than backward?' Explain that the radial oscillation frequency is reduced by (1 - 6M/r0)^{1/2}, so the particle needs more than 2 pi of azimuth to return to perihelion.

When restoring units, have the learner compute GM_sun/c^2 (about 1.5 km) first, then 6 pi GM/(c^2 a(1 - e^2)) and the number of orbits per century; comparing 41 with 43 arcseconds is a good lesson about which length enters the formula.
Address the rubber-sheet picture explicitly after the Mercury calculation: spatial curvature accounts for only about a third of the precession; the rest comes from how clock rates vary with radius.

For advanced learners, offer Exercise 23.7 as a coding task and suggest integrating u'' + u = M/L^2 + 3M u^2 to avoid square-root sign switching; for novices, use the interactive potential-plus-orbit demo instead.
Forward link: once massive orbits are clear, ask what changes if the particle is massless (drop the -1 in the normalization); this sets up Chapter 24 and the photon sphere at 3M.
